plan.topic: What is amylin? The 'second fullness hormone' behind the new combo weight-loss drugs
plan.angle: One sharp idea: GLP-1 isn't the only gut and pancreas fullness signal. Amylin is released with insulin after meals. It slows stomach emptying and signals 'full' to the brain. That's why the newest drugs pair it with GLP-1 (CagriSema, EloraTZP), or try it alone (petrelintide). Use one verified number from L1 with its arm and population: 'up to 23.3%, top dose, adults with T2D, phase 2b, 48 weeks'. Say on screen: 'investigational, not approved as of Sept 2026'. Point viewers to the full video. Add the exact prescriber line. Aim for 35–50s.

package.title: EloraTZP vs Tirzepatide: 23.3% vs 14.8% Weight Loss at 48 Wks #shorts
package.description:
Amylin is your pancreas's "enough" hormone. Meet the amylin + GLP-1 combos in trials now. In a Phase 2b trial of 367 adults with overweight/obesity and type 2 diabetes, Lilly reported 23.3% average weight loss on EloraTZP's top dose at 48 weeks vs 14.8% on tirzepatide 15 mg and 3% on placebo, if everyone had stayed on treatment. More people stopped for side effects (11–27% across combo doses vs ~3% on tirzepatide alone). Investigational, not approved as of Sept 2026.

factcheck.summary: I checked every claim against its primary source and they hold up. Hay et al., Pharmacol Rev 2015, confirms the physiology: amylin is released with insulin from beta cells, slows stomach emptying and promotes fullness. Lilly's release (PR Newswire, 30 Sept 2026) matches the script's numbers: phase 2b, 367 adults with obesity or overweight plus type 2 diabetes, 48 weeks, efficacy estimand. Top dose (eloralintide 9 mg + tirzepatide 15 mg) gave 23.3%, tirzepatide 15 mg 14.8% and placebo 3.0%. Stopping because of side effects was 10.8–27.0% on the combos vs 2.9% on tirzepatide. Side effects were mostly stomach-related and mostly during dose escalation, and the drug is still investigational. Zealand's release (5 Mar 2026) confirms petrelintide is an amylin analog tested on its own in Phase 2. REDEFINE 1 (Garvey, NEJM 2025, PMID 40544433) exists as cited. The framing is right: investigational status, top dose, estimand, comparators, population and the prescriber line are all there. The title delivers what it promises. Three small fixes are below: placebo context for stopping rates, a date hedge for CagriSema (FDA decision expected Q4 2026) and a tighter loop line.

issues.claim: more people stopped treatment because of side effects: 11 to 27% across combo doses vs about 3% on tirzepatide alone
issues.problem: The numbers match Lilly's release, but the placebo arm is missing. Lilly reports 16.7% of the placebo group stopped because of side effects, which suggests small arms and noisy rates. Our craft rules say every rate gets its placebo context.
issues.fix: Replace the narration with: "The catch: more people stopped treatment because of side effects: 11 to 27% across combo doses vs about 3% on tirzepatide alone (17% on placebo, in small groups)."

issues.problem: CagriSema was filed with the FDA in Dec 2025 and a US decision is expected in Q4 2026. Calling it investigational is accurate today but could go out of date within weeks, so it needs a date hedge.
issues.fix: Change the narration to: "So newer drugs, none approved as of September 2026, pair an amylin mimic with GLP-1 drugs, like CagriSema and Lilly's EloraTZP, or use it solo, like petrelintide." Change on_screen_text to: "Amylin + GLP-1 (not approved, Sept 2026)"

issues.problem: The line is loose. It could be read as saying GLP-1 medicines don't work without amylin, which contradicts the tirzepatide-alone results in s5. Rewording it removes that reading and keeps the loop.
issues.fix: Replace "GLP-1 never worked alone." with "Your GLP-1 always had a partner."
